problem:
LeetCode 252: Meeting Rooms
Function signature: canAttendMeetings(intervals)

data.title: Meeting Rooms
data.summary:
Input: An array of meeting time intervals where each interval consists of a start and end time.
Output: True if a person could attend all meetings without any overlap, and false otherwise.
Rules: Overlapping intervals include cases where one meeting starts exactly when another ends if considered conflicting, but typically standard interval overlap means if start[i] < end[j] and start[j] < end[i].

data.key_insight: If we sort the meetings by their start times, any overlapping meetings will appear consecutively in the sorted list. Thus, we only need to check if the start time of the current meeting is strictly less than the end time of the previous meeting.

steps.title: Check Edge Cases
steps.detail: If the intervals list is empty or has only one meeting, a person can trivially attend all meetings, so return true.

steps.title: Sort Intervals
steps.detail: Sort the meetings based on their start times in ascending order.

steps.title: Iterate and Check Overlaps
steps.detail: Loop through the sorted intervals starting from the second meeting. Compare its start time with the end time of the previous meeting. If the current start time is less than the previous end time, an overlap occurs, so return false.

steps.title: Return Success
steps.detail: If the loop completes without finding any overlaps, return true.

data.pattern_summary: Sorting intervals by their start or end times allows you to process them in a predictable order, making it easy to detect overlaps by comparing adjacent elements.

pattern_options.name: Sorting Intervals
pattern_options.feedback: Correct. Ordering the intervals helps detect overlaps efficiently by only needing to compare adjacent meetings.

pattern_options.name: Two pointers
pattern_options.feedback: Two pointers are usually used for searching pairs in sorted arrays or moving inwards from ends, not for checking interval overlaps.

pattern_options.name: Hash map lookup
pattern_options.feedback: Hash maps are useful for finding frequencies or complements in O(1) time, but intervals require ordered checks rather than direct key lookups.

pattern_options.name: Breadth-First Search
pattern_options.feedback: BFS is used for traversing graphs or trees level by level, which does not apply to simple linear interval arrays.

signals.phrase: An array of meeting time intervals
signals.hint: Implies you are dealing with range data that might overlap in arbitrary order.
Indicates you need to check pairs for conflicting time ranges.

data.brute_force_idea: Compare every possible pair of meetings to see if their time ranges intersect. If any pair overlaps, return false.
data.brute_force_why: There are nested loops comparing every meeting against every other meeting, resulting in a quadratic number of comparisons.
data.bottleneck: Comparing every meeting with every other meeting redundantly checks pairs in arbitrary order.
bottleneck_hints: Look at how the meetings are ordered when they are given to you.
If you know where meetings start relative to each other, do you need to check every single pair?
Think about what happens if you arrange the meetings chronologically first.

data.overview: This algorithm determines if a person can attend all meetings without overlapping by sorting the intervals by their start times. Once sorted, any conflict will occur between adjacent meetings, allowing us to compare each meeting's start time with the previous meeting's end time.
data.intuition: Imagine sorting your daily calendar events chronologically from earliest to latest. If event B starts before event C has finished, you have a scheduling conflict.

data.insight: The brute-force solution compares every pair of intervals, resulting in redundant work. By sorting the intervals by their start times first, we align them in chronological order. This means we only need to compare each meeting with the immediately preceding one to detect overlaps, removing the need for nested loops.

derivation.note: Sorting the intervals array dominates the time complexity.
A single loop iterates through the sorted intervals from index 1 to the end.
Comparing the current start time with the previous end time takes constant time.

data.time_summary: Line 13 takes O(n log n) time due to sorting. The loop from line 14 to 16 runs in O(n) time because it scans the list once. Combining these gives O(n log n) + O(n), which simplifies to O(n log n) overall.
data.space_summary: Python's Timsort algorithm uses O(n) auxiliary space to store references during the sort. If sorting in-place were guaranteed, it would be O(1), but standard list sorting requires O(n) space.
data.takeaway: When dealing with interval problems, always sort by start time first. This converts an all-pairs comparison problem into a linear scan.
mistakes: Failing to handle empty input lists, leading to IndexError when checking index 0.
Assuming intervals are already sorted and attempting to compare adjacent items without sorting.
Writing a nested loop (O(n^2)) instead of sorting and scanning in O(n log n).
